stories.title: Losing Your Licence Now Hurts More Than a Fine
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is making bad driving punishments tougher — losing your licence for weeks can sting more than paying money!
summary: In Singapore, every time a driver breaks a traffic rule — like speeding or running a red light — they get 'demerit points'. Think of it like a warning card in a game. Collect too many cards, and you get sent off the road for a while.

Now, drivers who reach a high number of demerit points face having their licence suspended, which means they cannot drive at all for a set time. Experts say this hurts drivers more than just paying a fine, because they cannot earn money or bring their families around without a car.

This rule also affects private-hire drivers, like those who drive for ride-hailing apps such as Grab. If they lose their licence, they lose their job for that time too, since driving is how they earn a living.

Some experts warn that a small group of 'habitual' risk-takers — people who keep breaking rules again and again — might not change their ways even with this stricter punishment. Singapore may need to find more ways to keep everyone safe on the road.

lenses.me: If you ride in a car, bus or Grab, safer drivers on the road mean a safer ride for you.
lenses.family: If a parent drives, this rule reminds them to follow traffic rules carefully — losing a licence could disrupt family plans like school pick-ups.
lenses.friends: Friends who take Grab or taxis to school might notice fewer risky drivers on Singapore's roads over time.
lenses.nation: Singapore wants to be known for safe, orderly roads, and stricter punishments help keep accidents down for everyone.
lenses.world: Many countries are watching how Singapore balances fines and licence suspensions to make roads safer — it could be a model for others.

stories.title: The Secret 'Think Tank' in Singapore That Wasn't Real
stories.headline_kid: A company in Singapore pretended to be a serious research group, but it may have actually been trying to secretly recruit people for foreign spy agencies.
summary: A 'think tank' is a group of smart people who research big problems, like a study club for grown-ups who write reports on politics or world events. A company in Singapore called Infoassa said it was one of these groups.

But when reporters checked, they found strange things. Infoassa had advertised at least six events over four months, but the most recent one on Aug 7 never actually happened. It also seemed to have fake employees.

One person who applied for a job there — a former US government worker — was asked to write about a real political meeting without using any information found online. Experts say this looks like a method foreign intelligence agencies use to find and recruit people who know useful secrets.
This story is a reminder that spying doesn't always look dramatic like in movies — it can hide behind ordinary-looking office buildings and job adverts, even in safe, orderly Singapore.

lenses.me: It teaches you to be careful and curious — not everything that looks official or impressive is actually real.
lenses.family: Parents can talk about how to spot suspicious job offers or 'too good to be true' opportunities.
lenses.friends: It's a good topic to discuss with friends about staying alert online and asking questions before trusting something.
lenses.nation: Because Singapore is a global hub with many important visitors and companies, it can also attract people trying to gather secrets — so staying alert matters for national security.
lenses.world: Countries everywhere use clever, hidden ways to gather information from each other, showing how spying has changed with technology and global connections.

stories.title: Why Petrol Might Get Pricier: A Sea Route Standoff
stories.headline_kid: Oil prices are climbing because a busy sea passage that carries much of the world's oil is still not fully open — and that could push up petrol prices here too.
summary: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow strip of sea between Iran and Oman. It's like a busy highway for giant ships called tankers, which carry huge amounts of oil from the Middle East to the rest of the world, including Singapore.

Iran has been blocking full use of this passage, and its Revolutionary Guards say they won't reopen it fully until the United States agrees to certain demands, including paying for war damages. Talks about new shipping routes with Oman are said to be close to finished, but the standoff continues.

Because so much of the world's oil passes through this one narrow strait, any blockage makes oil harder to get, which pushes prices up everywhere — even in Singapore, which is a major fuel port and imports much of its energy.
Higher oil prices can mean higher prices for petrol, bus and taxi fares, and even goods that need to be transported by trucks and ships, touching almost every family's daily budget.

lenses.me: If your family drives or takes Grab often, you might notice slightly higher costs for rides.
lenses.family: Household bills for petrol, transport and even groceries (which need to be delivered) could rise a little.
lenses.friends: Friends whose parents drive to work may hear grown-ups talking about rising petrol costs at home.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies heavily on imported oil and its position as a shipping hub, so global oil disruptions affect our economy directly.
lenses.world: Tensions in one small sea passage can ripple out and affect prices and businesses in almost every country on Earth.

stories.title: Thailand Mourns a Young Girl Lost in a School Tragedy
stories.headline_kid: A 12-year-old girl who was badly hurt in a shooting at a Thai school has sadly passed away, bringing the number of people who died to nine.
summary: Last week, a 14-year-old boy in Thailand shot his grandparents at home, then went to his school and hurt many students and teachers before the tragedy ended. It has become one of Thailand's worst school shootings in years.

Sadly, over the weekend, a 12-year-old girl named Naphat Chaima, who had been badly hurt, passed away in hospital. This raised the total number of deaths to nine, with several other people still recovering from serious injuries.

Dozens of grieving students, parents and teachers gathered at a Buddhist temple to pray and say goodbye to her. Police investigating the case found that the boy had watched violent videos online and learned how to use a gun from social media, even though a teacher had taken away an air gun from him a year earlier.

This heartbreaking event has made many people in Thailand talk about making gun rules stricter and being more careful about what children watch online. In Singapore, we're lucky to have very strict gun control laws, which help keep our schools and communities safe.

lenses.me: It's okay to feel sad or unsettled reading about this — talking to a trusted adult about your feelings always helps.
lenses.family: This is a good moment for families to talk about school safety and what to watch out for online.
lenses.friends: Friends may also feel worried; it helps to remind each other that Singapore's schools have strong safety rules.
lenses.nation: Singapore's strict laws about owning guns are one big reason why such tragedies are extremely rare here.
lenses.world: This tragedy is pushing countries to think harder about gun safety rules and how children access violent content online.

stories.title: Football Star Messi Says Goodbye to the Father Who Guided Him
stories.headline_kid: Football superstar Lionel Messi is mourning the loss of his father Jorge, the man who guided his amazing career since he was a little boy.
summary: Lionel Messi is one of the greatest footballers in history, having won the World Cup and eight Ballon d'Or awards — trophies given to the world's best player each year, a bit like being crowned 'Player of the Year' worldwide.
Behind his success was his father, Jorge Messi, who managed his career since childhood, much like a coach and manager rolled into one. Jorge passed away after battling cancer, at the age of 68.

Messi flew home to Argentina on a private flight with his wife Antonela and their children to attend the funeral. A quiet, private ceremony was held with close family and friends to say their final goodbyes.

Football is loved by millions in Singapore too, from young players at school CCAs to fans who cheer for their favourite teams. Messi's story reminds us that behind every great achievement, there's often someone — a parent, coach or family member — quietly supporting and believing in us.

lenses.me: It's a reminder to appreciate the people who support your own dreams, like parents, coaches or teachers.
lenses.family: It's a chance to think about and thank the family members who guide and support you, just like Jorge did for Messi.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might enjoy talking about your favourite footballers and what makes them special.
lenses.nation: Singapore has a growing football culture, with fans following stars like Messi and hoping to build our own football stories.
lenses.world: Fans across the globe, including many in Singapore, are sending messages of support to Messi, showing how sport connects people everywhere.
